summary: Specifies the PINT Service Protocol 1.0, which extends SIP and SDP so that a user on an IP network can invoke certain telephone services, such as asking for a call to be placed. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: You click a button on a web page and a real phone somewhere starts ringing. This defines the messages that let the Internet ask the phone network to do that.

questions: how to request a phone call from the internet
what is request to call in pint
how does sip trigger a phone call
what is the tn network type in sdp
subtitle: SIP and SDP extended so an IP host can ask the telephone network to place a call, send a fax or read out content.

tldr.problem: People wanted to trigger telephone services, such as a callback from a support desk or a fax of a document, from an IP network, but there was no standard way to send that request into the telephone network.
tldr.mechanism: PINT carries the request as a SIP invitation to a PINT gateway, with an SDP body describing the telephone session. It adds a telephone network type, data object references, context attributes, a require attribute and SUBSCRIBE, NOTIFY and UNSUBSCRIBE for monitoring.
tldr.outcome: A PINT client can ask for a call, a fax or spoken content, and optionally follow the result. Security is demanding: PINT messages MUST be protected from interception, modification and replay.

facts.label: Required to support
facts.value: TN with RFC2543 addresses, and the require attribute

today: RFC 2848 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is written against SIP as specified in RFC 2543 and SDP as in RFC 2327.

sections.title: Invoking Telephone Services From the Internet
sections.content:
RFC 2848 specifies PINT Service Protocol 1.0. The generic scenario has three steps: an IP host sends a request to a server on an IP network, the server relays the request into a telephone network, and the telephone network performs the call service. A PINT service always involves two networks: an IP network to request the call, and the Global Switched Telephone Network (GSTN) to carry it out.

The requirements were deliberately restricted to three milestone services. Request to Call makes a phone call connecting party A to party B. Request to Fax Content sends a fax to fax machine B, with the data pointed to or included in the request. Request to Speak/Send/Play Content calls a user and has content spoken out. The fax service is not 'Fax over IP': the IP network only carries the request.

PINT does not define the telephone-side details. Which call-center agent is chosen, whether the agent's phone rings first, and the fax protocol negotiation are all outside its scope.
sections.eli5: It lets a computer ask the phone company to do three things: ring someone, send a fax, or read something aloud over the phone. How the phone company does it is its own business.

sections.title: How PINT Builds on SIP and SDP
sections.content:
PINT clients and servers are SIP clients and servers. SIP carries the request over the IP network, and SDP describes the telephone session to be invoked. A user invites a remote PINT server into a session, and the SDP body says what should happen, for example a telephone call or sending a fax. Accepting the invitation is no guarantee that the media will be transported successfully.

Somewhere in a cloud of proxy, redirect and location servers sits a PINT gateway, which relays requests into the telephone system. To SIP it looks like a User Agent Server. Behind it is an Executive System that actually invokes services in the telephone network, and that is outside the scope of PINT.

Only two things MUST be supported by every PINT 1.0 client and server: the TN network type with its RFC2543 address type, and the require attribute. Everything else is optional, so an implementation that offers only Request-to-Call is allowed. Any SIP or SDP feature, such as the a=lang attribute or the t= time field, remains available unchanged.
sections.eli5: PINT reuses the messages that Internet phone calls already use. A special helper at the edge, the gateway, takes the note and passes it to the phone company.

sections.title: Telephone Addresses and Media in SDP
sections.content:
PINT adds the network type TN (Telephone Network) to SDP. Its address types are RFC2543, followed by a telephone-subscriber string, or private types that MUST begin with X-. A string starting with a plus sign is a global number, by default an E.164 number. One without it is a local number in the default dialling plan of the receiving gateway. Examples are c= TN RFC2543 +1-201-406-4090 and c= TN RFC2543 12014064090.

In the media line, the media type can be any discrete MIME top-level type, such as text, image or application. The port field has no meaning and is normally 1; 0 can mean the terminal is not receiving media, for example on hold. The transport protocol field takes voice, fax or pager, which says how the result is treated in the telephone network. The format field lists MIME sub-types, preferred first, or a single dash for a default. So m=audio 1 voice followed by a dash asks for a voice call using whatever audio the Executive System chooses.

The transport protocol does not dictate the media type: a text source with voice transport means text-to-speech over the phone.
sections.eli5: The note says who to call, using a phone number, and how to deliver the thing: as a voice call, a fax or a pager message.

sections.title: Data Objects and the fmtp Attribute
sections.content:
A request may refer to a data object to be faxed or spoken. Each format entry in the media line MUST be followed by an a=fmtp attribute that lists the sources. When several are listed they are sent in sequence. Three kinds of reference exist, each with its own tag.

  • uri: points to something on the IP network. It SHOULD be an absolute URI, for example a=fmtp:plain uri:ftp://ftp.isi.edu/in-notes/rfc2468.txt.
  • opr: is an opaque reference to something held in the telephone network. It passes through PINT untouched, and may be empty when the content is implied, as in a fax-back service defined by the number dialled.
  • spr: names the Content-ID of another MIME part inside the same request.

For included data, the request body is multipart MIME. The first part MUST hold the SDP, and multipart/related is recommended. Because a proxy might fork a request carrying a lot of data, such requests SHOULD be sent via TCP, and if the gateway location is unknown and the data would need several IP datagrams, the first request SHOULD carry a reference instead.
sections.eli5: The note can say 'use the picture at this web address', 'use item 123 you already have', or 'it is stapled to this note'.

sections.title: Context Attributes and the require Attribute
sections.content:
Some numbers only make sense in context, such as a freephone number reachable from limited networks, or a number only dialable inside one network or PBX. The a=phone-context attribute supplies that context: +972 means the number is in Israel, while X-acme.com-23 could name a private PBX network. Context values that are not registered with IANA MUST begin with X-.

The a=clir:true or false attribute says whether the caller's number may be shown to the other party. Executive Systems are not obliged to act on it in all territories. Attributes of the form a=Q763-nature, a=Q763-plan and a=Q763-INN map to fields of the ITU-T Q.763 CalledPartyAddress.

Since SDP lets servers ignore unknown attributes, a client SHOULD list those it insists on with a=require:. A server that does not recognise a listed attribute MUST return an error such as 420 or 400. If it recognises it but cannot honour it, it MUST reject the request with 606 Not Acceptable. To make sure the server even understands require, the client SHOULD add the SIP header Require: org.ietf.sdp.require.
sections.eli5: Some phone numbers only work from certain places, so the note can add 'dial this as if you are in this country' or 'insist on this or refuse'.

sections.title: Monitoring a Service Request
sections.content:
A requester often is not a party to the resulting call, so PINT adds three SIP methods. SUBSCRIBE opens a monitoring session, NOTIFY lets the gateway report changes, and UNSUBSCRIBE closes the session. Their state machine mirrors INVITE and BYE.

A SUBSCRIBE identifies the service session by the SDP origin field of the original request. It should carry an Expires header, and a value of 0 asks for one immediate answer. A gateway only has to keep state for as long as it said it would; after that, a SUBSCRIBE gets 606 Not Acceptable with Warning 307. The client SHOULD send SUBSCRIBE immediately before the ACK that confirms the service if it wants transient status. NOTIFY carries an updated session description and may carry a Warning header and an i= line such as '3 pages of 5 sent'. Unlike SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE can be sent by a gateway.

A BYE should end the telephone call if it can, but a fax may already be in progress or finished. Then the server MUST return 606 Not Acceptable to the BYE with a session description explaining the problem.
sections.eli5: You can ask 'tell me how the call goes'. The gateway sends progress messages like 'three pages of five sent', and either side can say 'that is enough'.

sections.title: PINT URLs, Warnings and Registration
sections.content:
The user part of a PINT SIP URL names the service. R2C, R2F and R2HC are reserved for the three milestone services, and other services MUST use other names. The host part is the service provider's domain. A new URL parameter tsp names the telephone service provider, as in sip:R2F@pint.pintservice.com;tsp=telco.com.

PINT servers MUST support the SIP Warning header, for instance to say a gateway cannot convert a jpeg for faxing. The Require header defines two PINT tags, org.ietf.sip.subscribe and org.ietf.sdp.require.

Gateways use ordinary SIP REGISTER to tell a proxy which services they offer, and several competing gateways may register for the same service. The RFC lists choices for a broker (overwrite, reject, keep all and fork or pick one) and leaves the policy outside PINT.
sections.eli5: The first part of the address says what you want, such as 'call me', and the rest says which company will do it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PINT request can cause a real phone call, so risks include a wrong or malicious number, harassment of an innocent third party, interception, or alteration of the request. Providers may need to confirm who is asking and whether they are authorised to pay. Authorisation data SHOULD be treated like a credit card number or PIN.

The summary is firm: PINT messages MUST be protected from interception, modification and replay, and implementations MUST support SIP security. Lower-layer protection such as IPsec or TLS may be used instead. The Request-URI and To: fields cannot be protected by SIP techniques, so if they are sensitive, transport or network-layer protection MUST be used. All registrations by gateways MUST be authenticated, otherwise a rogue operator could spoof or hijack another provider's service name. Encrypted bodies also stop proxies choosing a gateway from the SDP, which opens a denial-of-service avenue, so service names should let proxies choose without reading it.
sections.eli5: Because the note makes a real phone ring and may cost money, it must be sealed so nobody can read it, change it or reuse it.
